items.body: The latest installment in the Portraits GRM series pairs the duo of crys cole & Oren Ambarchi with Italian maestro Giuseppe Ielasi. Each occupying a full side of vinyl, the result is a document of where contemporary sound practice finds itself in 2026 while paying homage to the institutional framework that made such work possible. This is not musique concrète in the traditional sense, but it is undeniably born from the same spirit of inquiry that drove Pierre Schaeffer to upend our relationship with sound nearly eighty years ago. Pierre Schaeffer (1910-1995) is remembered not necessarily for his music, or even his philosophical contributions to the study of sound (which were significant), but for his institution building. After pioneering musique concrète while working in French radio in the late 1940s and early 1950s, Schaeffer began almost instantly institutionalizing his legacy, what became the Groupe de Recherches Musicales (GRM) in 1958 (known as Ina-GRM since 1975). The tension between preserving a tradition and remaining open to the new has defined the institution ever since. My 2019 interview with François J. Bonnet—composer, philosopher, and current director of Ina-GRM—explored precisely this question: how does an institution honor its past while making space for the unfamiliar? An answer arrived in 2020 with the launch of Portraits GRM, a series of commissioned releases designed to bring contemporary voices into the GRM’s hallowed studios. The first release was Jim O’Rourke’s Shutting Down Here, fittingly so, as his sessions there spanned 30 years and thus that work’s completion constituted the closing of a significant loop. The re-issuing of classic and adjacent GRM titles began under the direction of Editions Mego, but after the death of Peter Rehberg (Pita) in 2021, the series transitioned to the stewardship of Shelter Press. Since then, Portraits GRM has featured Lucy Railton, Okkyung Lee, Kali Malone, Lasse Marhaug, Laurel Halo, Beatrice Dillon, and many others—artists who share little aesthetically but are united by a willingness to push against the boundaries of what sound can do. As with most installments in the series, the latest release offers two compelling sidelong works from heavyweights of the experimental underground. On one side, crys cole and Oren Ambarchi continue their collaborative exploration of texture and density; on the other, Giuseppe Ielasi presents something distinctly his own. crys cole & Oren Ambarchi ~ Sparkling or Silent The title suggests something binary—a flickering between presence and absence, articulation and withholding—but the piece itself operates in the spaces between. Sparkling or Silent opens with what might best be described as ASMR-concrète: close-mic’d rustling, breath, the micro-articulations of objects manipulated in near-silence. It is intimate yet abstract, as though the listener has stumbled upon a private ritual. Over its 19’43’’ duration, the work unfolds in several distinct movements, each building upon the last until the accumulated density becomes something else entirely. Oren Ambarchi needs little introduction. The Australian guitarist has built a formidable reputation as a solo artist and one of the most prolific collaborators in experimental music, with a discography that touches on everything from the glacial drone of his solo work to the rhythmic propulsion of his trio with Johan Berthling and Andreas Werliin—whose Ghosted series has only grown more assured with each installment. Records including Grapes from the estate (2004), Hubris (2016), and Simian Angel (2019) are personal favorites, not to mention his ongoing dialogues with figures like Keiji Haino and Jim O’Rourke. But alongside this celebrated career, there exists another body of work, equally significant if less discussed: his partnership with crys cole. Likely the less familiar name to many listeners, cole’s work is no less deserving of attention. I have been a fan of this Canadian sound artist’s practice for years, both in her solo work and her collaborations. Her third album for Black Truffle, Making Conversation collects three recent commissioned pieces and demonstrates a trajectory that has moved steadily toward greater formal control without sacrificing the tactile, almost sculptural quality of her sound. She had been involved with Winnipeg’s send + receive festival for over a decade, contributed photographs and projections to classic Canadian experimental records, and continues to be an active performer and sound artist. Her work with Ora Clementi—the duo with James Rushford—offers a dense thicket of sonic material that feels both organic and constructed. Sylva Sylvarum, in particular, stands as a high-water mark in her collaborative output. On Ambarchi’s Audience of One (2012), she’s credited as contributing contact microphones and brushes to the track “Passage.” They’ve since produced several records as a duo: Sonja Henies Vei 31 (2014), a hazy collage of intimate gesture and field recordings from a Norwegian sojourn; Hotel Record (2017), its title a dryly witty reference to its origins in hotel room sessions, a study in digital textures; and Gallivant (2021), documenting a live concert from the previous year. The pair have often played with others, including Keith Rowe and Leif Elggren. The collaborative dynamic is worth dwelling on, if only because there is something peculiar and generative about a musical duo that is also a romantic couple. One thinks of the historical precedents: Sonny and Linda Sharrock, whose volatile partnership produced some of the most ferocious free jazz of the late 1960s and early 1970s; Max Roach and Abby Lincoln, whose work together addressed civil rights with a moral urgency that still resonates, again overshadowed by a documented history of abuse. More recently, and hopefully less problematically, I think of Christina Vantzou and John Also Bennett, Matmos (MC Schmidt and Drew Daniel), and Two-Way Street—Ashlee Booth on cello and Adam Lion on percussion, for whom Sarah Hennies wrote a piece exploring precicely the dynamic between a romantic and musical partnership. Giuseppe Ielasi and Jennifer Veillerobe have even released a few short pieces as Eselsohr. There is something about the intimacy of shared life that translates into the shared space of improvisation and composition, a trust that allows for risk without the safety net of distance. A residency abroad, a portrait of two artists developing a shared vocabulary in confined spaces, the energy of a live recording. Sparkling or Silent represents something different—a consciously composed concert work. As the Portraits GRM materials describe it, the piece is “a moment apart in their respective artistic approaches” where an electroacoustic method that has always been latent in both of their practices “here asserts itself as a central compositional modality.” This shift from documentation to composition makes Sparkling or Silent feel more expansive and considered, even if it doesn’t necessarily represent a linear “evolution” so much as a deliberate side-step into a different mode of working. From its intimate opening, Sparkling or Silent gradually accumulates tonal densisty before dissolving again. About halfway through, after cohering into a sustained drone cloud, the texture thins; ghostly melodies and gentle rustlings emerge from the haze, while field recordings slowly ground us in an unexpected place. The real surprise arrives in the final four minutes: a sudden chorus of truck (?) horn harmonies. The effect recalls Alvin Curran’s Maritime Rites, transposed from water to asphalt; the collective ritual of Curran’s foghorns replaced by the found sounds of the highway. Within a minute, these sounds accumulate into a dense, surprisingly consonant cluster, overlapping blares forming a sustained fog of noise that continues until, finally, the sparkle turns to silence. It is a closing gesture that reframes everything that came before, revealing the delicate rustlings of the opening as part of a larger soundscape that extends far beyond the studio walls. The piece does not so much end as disperse, its constituent parts returning to the world from which they were borrowed.   Giuseppe Ielasi ~ unfamiliar music (paris) In Milano in 2017, I met Giuseppe Ielasi and Jennifer Veillerobe for dinner accompanied by Oren and crys, who were part-time residents of the city then—their European headquarters, before relocating to Berlin, was this underrated Italian metropolis, a base between their Australian and Canadian homelands. So in my mind, the connection between the artists featured on this record is obvious, forged not only through shared aesthetics but through shared meals, shared cities, shared lives. But Ielasi’s relationship to this series extends far beyond personal connections. He has mastered every Portraits GRM record except the first, and his own Senufo label released early records by Kassel Jaeger, which was in fact my introduction to François J. Bonnet many years ago. This record, then, feels like a culmination; the current director of Ina-GRM, the mastering engineer, the series, and the artists all intertwined in a web of mutual influence and respect that spans decades. Ielasi’s catalog is deep and varied, marked by a restless curiosity that refuses to settle into comfortable routines. He has his interests and proclivities—a fascination with small sounds, repetition, motors, unusual rhythmic grooves, in other words “an insistence on material”—but he rarely deploys the same technical setup or approach twice, constantly searching for new means of expression. This commitment to renewal is evident throughout his discography, from his early work on the 12k label to his more recent return to explorations of guitar and electronics. unfamiliar music (paris) arrives with some precedent. Ielasi has performed at the GRM before; I have a recording from 20 January 2014 at GRM Paris that captures his take on acousmatic diffusion. The title itself is shared with unfamiliar music vol.1 (guitar duets), a 2024 digital record that expanded a renewed focus on guitar as a sound source that began with releases in 2020. But what connection does this new piece have to that earlier work? The title seems to refer less to a specific genre or instrumentation and more to a mode of production, an approach to working with sound that prioritizes the strange, the dislocated, the not-quite-familiar. The cover of this release depicts Ielasi performing in Paris with a sampler, suggesting a process rooted in improvisation and constraint. And indeed, some of the samples in the piece do seem to be shared with previously released works, here recontextualized and repurposed. This is not a work of pure creation ex nihilo but of rearrangement, of finding new relationships between existing materials, a practice that echoes both the concrète tradition as well as Ielasi’s own history of pushing it into new territory. The GRM’s acousmatic tradition is evident in the microphone technique and in the spatial treatment of sounds, but there is also a digital air to the proceedings that feels distinctly contemporary, a reminder that the techniques Schaeffer pioneered have been absorbed, transformed, and rendered nearly invisible in the work of subsequent generations. Where cole and Ambarchi’s contribution moves from intimacy to surreal mundanity, Ielasi’s work operates in a different register entirely. The piece itself unfolds as a study in gentle contrast and rhythmic accumulation. The rhythmic elements that have long characterized his work are present but transformed—pulses that never quite lock into a predictable groove, small sounds that build into larger textures, a sense of propulsion that constantly threatens to derail itself. Static gives way to layers of competing rhythm gives way to a mobile lullaby. unfamiliar music (paris) passes through a range of sonic territories without any clear delineations between movements. Ielasi opts instead for a gradual process of substitution. What emerges is a piece that feels both of its moment and somehow outside of it. The “unfamiliar” of the title is not a description of the sounds themselves but of the relationships between them, the way they refuse to settle into expected patterns or resolve into comfortable listening. Ielasi makes music that demands attention without demanding understanding, that rewards close listening without promising easy rewards.   Taken together with the cole and Ambarchi piece, this release offers a portrait of the series at its best: two works that share little in common but are united by a willingness to push against the boundaries of what sound can do, and a commitment to the kind of exploration that Schaeffer himself would have recognized. The Portraits GRM series continues to honor its institutional legacy not through preservation but through renewal, not by looking backward but by making space for the unfamiliar. (Joseph Sannicandro)

items.body: New York-based musician Edley ODowd, formerly of Psychic TV, will release his second solo album, “Kowai-Yet,” on November 26, 2026 via the French label Arsenic Solaris. The ambient and experimental record follows his 2022 debut, “F(our)-Ward,” and arrives on vinyl and digital, with the Pink LP edition limited to 200 copies. ODowd recorded “Kowai-Yet” over three years in multiple locations. The album brings together material he made with collaborators he has worked with since leaving New York City to live closer to nature five years ago. The seven-track record shifts from the sound-collage approach of “F(our)-Ward” toward a more emotional register. “Where F(our)-Ward was more about sound collage, Kowai-Yet is about emotion,” ODowd says. “It’s infused with joy as well as a heaping dose of sadness.” The album’s title traces back to a single word. Describing a drive home on a summer night, ODowd recalls the sound of crickets against his car tires on humid pavement as both “sinister but compelling.” The Japanese word “kowai,” meaning “scary,” came to him first. At a stop sign, as the air went still, “quiet” followed, and the two merged into “Kowai-yet.” Individual tracks trace separate origins. “Heat” took shape through an improvised studio session in Los Angeles with engineer Joo Joo Ashworth, built from a drum pattern and expanded with analog electronics set against ODowd’s backwards saxophone. “Again” began as a more traditional song ODowd wrote alone. British musician Gore Tech later added a sharper beat, two guitarists contributed parts, and singer Zoah, whom ODowd met at a coffee shop along the Delaware River, added vocals and lyrics. “Arbiter” reworks stems ODowd had originally recorded for an unfinished song about his friend Lady Jaye Breyer P-Orridge. Its choruses use samples recorded during a 2000 trip to Nepal with Lady Jaye and Genesis P-Orridge, manipulated into the track. His Problem Addict collaborator Andrew Mann closes the song with guitar feedback. “Kowai-Yet” tracklist: 1. “Jamesey” 2. “Arbiter” 3. “Again” 4. “(Bruce Was) Kicked Out Of The Band” 5. “Heat” 6. “Sunrise” 7. “You’ll Never Know” Kowai-Yet release details “Kowai-Yet” is out November 26, 2026 via Arsenic Solaris as a digital album and a Pink LP limited to 200 copies. Both are available to pre-order on Bandcamp, where the track “Heat” is streaming now. Photo credits: Trevor Gregory. Kowai-Yet by Edley ODowd About Edley ODowd Edley ODowd grew up in the suburbs outside New York City and moved to Manhattan in the late 1980s, shortly after finishing high school. He got his start on a secondhand drum kit his mother bought him at a garage sale when he was 13. During a semester abroad in London in 1991, he joined the shoegaze band The Butterflies. Back in New York, he played drums and DJed for Toilet Boys, a band that wound down after a major European tour supporting the Red Hot Chili Peppers. In 2003, ODowd was instrumental in reviving Psychic TV, persuading Genesis P-Orridge to perform again. The reunited band’s first show took place at The Coral Room in New York City on December 5, 2003. ODowd founded the label Angry Love Productions after a self-funded Psychic TV EP sold out its 230 copies within two weeks. The “PTV3” lineup of Psychic TV played its final show on November 15, 2018. Alongside music, ODowd has worked as a graphic designer for major labels since 1993, taught courses at several universities in the late 1990s and early 2000s, and worked as a mental health counselor, including as a front-line worker during the COVID-19 pandemic. ODowd released his debut solo album, “F(our)-Ward,” as a self-released, ultra-limited cassette via Flesh Prison/DeathBed Tapes in 2022. Side-Line covered its expanded reissue, “F(our) ward,” released as a trifold-sleeved CD with three bonus tracks via the Italian label 13 on February 23, 2023. That same year, ODowd formed the death rock band Scorpion Tea with Christian Cruz, singer Anthony Diaz and bassist Fern Puma, signing to the label GIVE/TAKE. Side-Line covered the band’s debut single, “Scarlet Misquote,” in June 2023, ahead of the band’s self-titled debut album. ODowd now lives about an hour’s drive from New York City, where he continues to split his time between graphic design clients, band rehearsals and recording. “Kowai-Yet,” his second solo album, is set for release on November 26, 2026 via Arsenic Solaris.

items.body: Israeli gothic metal band Fatum Aeternum has rebuilt “P.W.Y.P.” for a streaming release, bringing the track back from their 2012 EP “The Sermon.” The self-released single went out digitally on 25 September 2026. The new version keeps the original ’80s glam-rooted guitar riff while adding aggressive male vocals, a female counter voice, cello and a full gospel choir. Where the 2012 recording leaned on social commentary, the rebuilt arrangement expands it into a more layered, theatrical gothic sound the band describes as a dark sermon. “P.W.Y.P.” is the second single in Fatum Aeternum’s renewed run of releases, following the comeback single “As Above, So Below” on 25 August 2026. That single introduced a new six-piece lineup – Steve Gershin, Evelyn Shor Gershin, Dr. Joe, Victor Grassiano, Max Datskovsky and Mark Muzykant – which also plays on “P.W.Y.P.” The track was recorded at Lodge Studios in Northampton, UK. Denis Saenko handled mixing and mastering, with additional mixing by Gershin; Tayo Olawepo arranged and recorded the choir. The band’s promotional materials cite Lacrimosa, Therion and Haggard as reference points. “P.W.Y.P.” is available to stream on Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube, Amazon Music, Deezer and SoundCloud. About Fatum Aeternum Fatum Aeternum formed in Tel Aviv, Israel, in 2006, built around Steve Gershin on mandolin, bass and vocals, alongside Ze’ev Gut on fiddle and vocals and Olga Braverman on flute and vocals. The group’s first full lineup added Ilya Surnin on drums, Dan Yoffe on guitar and Rivka Aizenberg on viola, playing a self-described “renaissance metal” blend of folk and metal. Braverman left in 2007 and Gut in 2008, staying on as a guest musician as the band shifted toward a heavier, more electrified sound. Gershin considered disbanding the group in 2009 and recorded a memorial album of earlier material instead; Evelyn Shor Gershin joined permanently around the same time, stabilising the lineup. The band re-recorded its debut album “This Dream Is Dead” several times before releasing it on CD in 2011. On 24 September 2011, Fatum Aeternum played the 12th Children of the Night Gothic Festival in Kyiv, Ukraine, its first show outside Israel, sharing the bill with Waves Under Water and Diary of Dreams. The video for “Apocalypse Now” followed on YouTube in April 2012 and aired on MTV Israel’s “Headbangers Ball” that June. The band self-released the EP “The Sermon” in September 2012, recorded at Lodge Studios in Northampton, UK, and opened for Apoptygma Berzerk the same month before going on hiatus in 2013. Gershin and Evelyn Shor Gershin rebuilt the lineup with George Falk and Igor May in 2014, releasing the single “One Bastard” that April and the maxi-single “The Pain” later the same year. The EP “The Darkest Hour” followed in 2015, then “Mass Suicide of Human Race” in 2017 and “Singing Songs of Desperation” in 2020. Fatum Aeternum returned in 2026 after a three-year gap, a pause the band’s own site attributes to health issues within the group. The comeback single “As Above, So Below” arrived on 25 August 2026 with a new six-piece lineup of Gershin, Evelyn Shor Gershin, Dr. Joe, Victor Grassiano, Max Datskovsky and Mark Muzykant. “P.W.Y.P.,” a rebuilt version of the 2012 “The Sermon” track, follows as the second single in that renewed run.

items.body: David J, a co-founder, bassist and co-songwriter of the post-punk bands Bauhaus and Love and Rockets, releases the single “Requiem for the Rose Garden” on 51 Recordings on 8 October 2026. The song is a protest aimed at the Trump administration, built around the White House Rose Garden as a target that is both symbolic and literal. It is the first track confirmed from J’s new album “Postcards from the Afterlife,” due 27 November on double LP, CD and digital formats. David J on ‘Requiem for the Rose Garden’ J points to physical changes made at the White House since Donald Trump’s first term in office when he explains the song. “It’s basically a protest about Trump’s administration and the atrocities it has visited upon the USA,” he said. “In the context of the song, the Rose Garden at the White House can be seen as a symbolic metaphor, although it is also quite literal. I actually wrote it during Trump’s first term in office when he had that beautiful garden hacked up. Now, even more horror has been inflicted on it of course, and the elegant East Wing of the building completely decimated which is also highly symbolic.” The backing band on the track is Duende, a Detroit-based group J has worked with extensively in the past. “Requiem for the Rose Garden” streams on Spotify, Apple Music, Tidal, Deezer and Pandora via davidjhaskins.com. ‘Postcards from the Afterlife’ due in November on 51 Recordings “Postcards from the Afterlife” is a 14-song album featuring a revolving cast of musicians and numerous autobiographical references. J sums up its themes as circling the same idea from several angles: “essentially about the poignant persistence of connection, be it in life or in death. Schisms and transitions. Love found and love lost. Requiems, reflection and revelation.” Several tracks carry string arrangements, including a finale recorded with members of the Prague Symphony and Philharmonic Orchestras. The rest of the album moves between soulful material, hazy 1960s orchestral pop, European-style chanson and the alternative rock territory J is best known for. “Postcards from the Afterlife” is released on double LP, CD and digital on 27 November. Tour dates for David J David J tours the UK through December 2026, with additional shows in Portugal, Germany and Greece around the “Postcards from the Afterlife” release. 27 November – Porto, Portugal 28 November – Lisbon, Portugal 1 December – London, UK – Moth Club 2 December – Reading, UK – Face Bar 4 December – Hebden Bridge, UK – Trades Club 5 December – Liverpool, UK – Rough Trade 8 December – Edinburgh, UK – The Voodoo Rooms 9 December – Glasgow, UK – Stereo 10 December – Newcastle, UK – The Cluny 11 December – Birmingham, UK – Hare & Hounds 13 December – Brighton, UK – Daltons 15 December – Athens, Greece – Death Disco 17 December – Berlin, Germany – Frannz Club About David J David J, born David John Haskins on 24 April 1957 in Northampton, England, co-founded Bauhaus in 1978, playing bass and co-writing songs including the group’s debut single, “Bela Lugosi’s Dead.” He sang lead vocals on “Who Killed Mr Moonlight?” Bauhaus split in 1983 and has reformed periodically since. Before Love and Rockets, J spent two years as bassist and co-producer for The Jazz Butcher, led by Pat Fish, working on the albums “A Scandal in Bohemia” (1984) and “Sex and Travel” (1985). He formed Love and Rockets in 1985 with fellow former Bauhaus members Daniel Ash and his younger brother Kevin Haskins, playing bass and sharing vocals and songwriting across seven albums released between 1985 and 1998. Both bands have reformed at intervals since their original breakups. J maintained a solo career alongside both bands. He released “Etiquette of Violence” in 1983, “Crocodile Tears and the Velvet Cosh” in 1985 and the singles compilation “On Glass” in 1986. His 1990 album “Songs from Another Season” produced the single “I’ll Be Your Chauffeur,” which reached number one on the Modern Rock Tracks chart. “Urban Urbane” followed in 1992, then “Estranged” in 2003, “Not Long for This World” in 2011 and “An Eclipse of Ships” in 2014. His memoir, “Who Killed Mister Moonlight? (Bauhaus, Black Magick and Benediction),” was published by Jawbone Press in 2014. In 2019 J released the double LP “Missive to an Angel From the Halls of Infamy and Allure.” Side-Line covered the album’s single “I Only Hear Silence Now,” featuring Emily Jane White, alongside a run of 2020 tour dates that included Bauhaus shows at Primavera Sound and Release Athens Festival. “What The Patrons Heard,” a ten-track set of originals and covers recorded over 34 years and first issued to Patreon subscribers, followed on CD and digital on 25 March 2022, with a limited numbered vinyl edition. J’s triple album of archival demos, “Tracks from the Attic,” was announced in February 2024 and released that year. He self-released the spoken-word album “The Mother Tree,” recorded with the band RAQIA, on 6 June 2025. He returned to the “Tracks from the Attic” material in March 2026 with a companion album, “Tracks From the Attic Revisited,” which Side-Line discussed with him the following month in the interview “David J Opens the Attic.” This month’s single and the album that follows continue that run of archival and new recordings.

The night is billed as “The Hotel presents…” and also features Rocheman and performance artist Finn Kennedy. Doors are at 7:30pm, with tickets priced from £13 for Café OTO members up to £20 on the door, available through the venue. The show is The Hotel’s third evening at Café OTO in 2026. Gilbert’s set previews a new album due from The Hotel later this year. Test pressings of the as-yet-unannounced record will be sold at the merch table. Finn Kennedy premieres a newly commissioned piece titled “Streams.” Rocheman closes the night with a full band set, performing as a quartet with Fred Lomas on lead guitar, Tom Powell on drums and Tom Wright on keyboards. Marias, producing the single “Drop/So” in 1980 for the group’s Dome label and co-producing the 1989 album “One of Our Girls (Has Gone Missing),” sharing songwriting credit with Angela Conway. items.body: German-Finnish futurepop duo PLATRONiC will release the three-track EP “The Emperor’s New Clothes” on 16 October 2026, with three new takes on their March single “Fortress of Fools.” The song started with a poem written by Kay Burden, inspired by Hans Christian Andersen’s “The Emperor’s New Clothes.” Kay originally had a storytelling ballad in mind. Then Sami Jumppanen presented her with a considerably more danceable instrumental, and “Fortress of Fools” became something else entirely. PLATRONiC build three new versions of ‘Fortress of Fools’ For the new EP, they have gone back to the song and, appropriately enough, given it three new “dresses.” The first, “The Dark Electro Country Dress,” is a collaboration with On Moral Ends, the Linköping-based electronic project of Swedish songwriter, singer and multi-instrumentalist Andreas Svensson. His work moves through different electronic and alternative styles, making the collaboration a rather unusual match for PLATRONiC’s futurepop side. For “The Synthpop Mashup Dress,” PLATRONiC worked with Finnish keyboardist, producer and remixer Imppu from Lahti. His work stretches from danceable synthpop to more cinematic electronic sounds, and he has also created remixes and reworks for former Kraftwerk member Wolfgang Flür. The third version stays with Kay and Sami themselves: “The Dark Medieval Gothic Dress.” According to PLATRONiC, “Fortress of Fools” spent several weeks in the Top 10 of both the Klangwald Charts and GEWC following its release earlier this year. The track reached #8 in the Klangwald Charts. The video for “Fortress of Fools” was filmed in Savonlinna, Finland, and Alicante, Spain, and was created and produced by PLATRONiC. PLATRONiC formed in 2020 and consists of German singer-songwriter and co-producer Kay Burden and Finnish composer and producer Sami Jumppanen. Side-Line readers may also know the duo from “How To Ride The Wave,” which appeared earlier this year on Side-Line’s The Freya Files Ukraine benefit compilation. “The Emperor’s New Clothes” tracklist: 1. “Fortress of Fools – The Dark Electro Country Dress” (PLATRONiC & On Moral Ends) 2. “Fortress of Fools – The Synthpop Mashup Dress” (PLATRONiC & Imppu) 3. “Fortress of Fools – The Dark Medieval Gothic Dress” (PLATRONiC) Before the three new “dresses” arrive, “Fortress of Fools” already has its own visual counterpart. “The Emperor’s New Clothes” is available to pre-save via DistroKid ahead of its 16 October release. About PLATRONiC PLATRONiC released the single “Now!” in June 2022, followed by the EP “The Healing” in April 2023 and a cover of Depeche Mode’s “The Things You Said” that August. A reworked version of their debut single “Pride” followed in June 2024, then the winter single “Winter Stores” that December. In March 2025, they released the teaser video for “How to Ride the Wave,” and in December 2025 contributed a cover of Depeche Mode’s “But Not Tonight” to the “In Your Memory 2” tribute compilation. “Fortress of Fools” followed in March 2026 as the duo’s most recent original single, ahead of “The Emperor’s New Clothes” EP arriving on 16 October.

items.body: Cleopatra Records will issue “Drink the New Wine”, the last studio recording by post-punk and goth rock band Bauhaus, as a 12-inch vinyl single on 30 October 2026. The pressing comes in three hand-numbered, etched color variants – white, silver and red – capped at 150 copies each, for a total of 450. Peter Murphy, Daniel Ash, David J and Kevin Haskins recorded the track separately during COVID-19 lockdown. The four traded audio files using the surrealist “exquisite corpse” method the band had used before. Bauhaus released it digitally in March 2022, its first new song since the 2008 album “Go Away White.” No Bauhaus recording has followed. Ash confirmed in April 2023 that the band’s reunion had ended, with the surviving members reforming Love and Rockets. ‘Drink the New Wine’: a lockdown recording now on hand-numbered vinyl Ash describes the track as typical of the band’s more playful side. “I always loved it when Bauhaus would go into art fart mode. Truly liberating and FUN!” he said. Cleopatra Records calls the release “a music artifact […] created for the most dedicated Bauhaus fans and collectors.” Side A of the single holds “Drink the New Wine.” Side B is etched with a reproduction of the Bauhaus logo and carries no audio. Each copy is individually hand-numbered, one color per customer, with no repressing planned once the 450 copies sell out. The single is available for pre-order through Cleopatra Records ahead of the 30 October release. About Bauhaus Small Wonder Records released Bauhaus’s debut single, “Bela Lugosi’s Dead,” in August 1979, a year after Peter Murphy, Daniel Ash, David J (David John Haskins) and his younger brother Kevin Haskins formed the band in Northampton, England. The single arrived before goth existed as a named scene. Four studio albums followed in four years on 4AD and Beggars Banquet: “In the Flat Field” (1980), “Mask” (1981), “The Sky’s Gone Out” (1982) and “Burning from the Inside” (1983). Bauhaus split on 5 July 1983, a week before “Burning from the Inside” reached shops. The pioneering band reunited for a 1998 tour and again from 2005 to 2008, a run that produced a fifth album, “Go Away White” (2008, Cooking Vinyl), released without a supporting tour. Ash, David J and Kevin Haskins had already carried their partnership into Love and Rockets, formed in 1985, and into separate solo careers. David J’s catalog includes the albums “Etiquette of Violence” and “Songs from Another Season,” plus a 2014 memoir, “Who Killed Mister Moonlight?” The four original members reunited again in 2019, announcing Peter Murphy’s first live date with Bauhaus after a heart attack ahead of shows at the Hollywood Palladium that November. A further reunion tour followed in 2022, covering Europe and the US West Coast. Months after the band released “Drink the New Wine,” Murphy’s rehab admission forced it to cancel the rest of its North American tour that August. Ash ended the reunion in April 2023, and the surviving trio returned to Love and Rockets. David J has stayed active since. He revisited his own archive on the album ‘Tracks From the Attic Revisited’ and discussed the project earlier this year in a Side-Line interview. This is the first time “Drink the New Wine” has been pressed to a physical format.

The track is the third single from the duo’s upcoming EP “Another Escape,” due November 5, and the release will be marked with a show at Semifinal in Helsinki the same day. It’s probably one of the most radio-friendly tracks we’ve ever made.” Decadence by I Think I Broke Something “Decadence” follows “Illegal,” released August 6, and “Heads Up,” released September 9, as the third single from “Another Escape” ahead of the EP’s November 5 release. “Decadence” is available as a digital single on Bandcamp and Spotify. About I Think I Broke Something I Think I Broke Something, also known as ITIBS, is a Helsinki-based duo made up of Jouni and Miika, active since 2014. The project debuted with the EP “Superman Sabotage Clan” and has since released three full-length albums, including “Still Not Going To,” announced for an October 26, 2022 release as the duo’s third LP, alongside numerous singles and remixes through various labels. items.body: Town & Towers Records releases Purwien & Kowa‘s new single “Italo-disco in San Francisco” on 9 October 2026, ahead of the German synth-pop duo’s sixth studio album, “Sechs,” due 23 October on the same label. The digital single carries four tracks: German and English versions of “Italo-disco in San Francisco,” an extended “Irgendwas ist immer (12″ Mix)” and a combined “German English Mashup 12″ mix” of the title track. Both language versions of the lyrics string together a run of 1980s references, naming figures including Lady Diana, Mikhail Gorbachev, Blondie, Phil Collins, Falco and Michael Jackson alongside songs such as “Blue Monday,” “Tainted Love,” “Like a Virgin,” “Take On Me,” “99 Luftballons,” “Forever Young” and “The Final Countdown.” “Italo-disco in San Francisco” mixes Italo disco, synthpop, New Wave and EBM, and follows the singles “Concorde” and “Hinter Glas” as the third preview of “Sechs.” Italo-disco in San Francisco by Purwien & Kowa About Purwien & Kowa Purwien & Kowa is a German synth-pop duo based in Dortmund formed by Christian Purwien and Thomas Kowa. Purwien co-founded the electronic/darkwave act Second Decay in 1987, initially under the name Blue Velvet, together with Andreas Michael Sippel. Second Decay released the tape “Monochromes” in 1988 and the 12-inch “Killing Desire” in 1989, followed by “La Décadence Électronique” on CD in 1992, the “Hinter Glas” maxi-CD in 1993 and the album “Taste” in 1994. The band continued with “Der Nerv” in 1995, “Familiar” in 1997, “The Hunt” and “De Luxe” in 1998, “Hotels” in 1999 and “Kaltes, weißes Licht” in 2001, before pausing new material after the 2002 live release “Zwischenfall 1999.” Thomas Kowa, born Thomas Kowalzik in 1969 in Ludwigshafen am Rhein, joined the German synth-pop band No Comment in 1989 and has lived in Switzerland since 2007. He founded the label Nanopop in 2001, closing it in 2007 to focus on writing. Since 2012 he has published a series of crime novels and thrillers. His other current music projects include Nine Seconds and Emily Kinski’s dead. Purwien and Kowa began recording together as Purwien & Kowa, releasing the three-EP digital set “Drei” via Zwei Records in October 2018. The duo also co-hosts the Disko 80 podcast, which covers 1980s music and has featured more than 100 episodes with guests including Joachim Witt, Bernhard Lloyd of Alphaville and Marcus Meyn of Camouflage. Kowa separately co-hosts the “Krimi Schweiz” podcast on Swiss crime fiction. Purwien and Kowa also record together as Heldautomat, whose own single “Liebe ist endlich” reached Town & Towers Records on the same day as “Italo-disco in San Francisco.” The duo performed at the 18th Elektrisch Festival in 2026. Purwien & Kowa returned this year with the singles “Concorde,” “Hinter Glas” and “Italo-disco in San Francisco,” ahead of their sixth studio album, “Sechs,” produced by Olaf Wollschläger and due 23 October 2026 via Town & Towers Records.

It is the third single from the Dortmund, Germany duo’s debut album “Zwischen den Lichtern”, due October 23 on the same label. “Liebe ist endlich” (“Love is finite”) opens with a slow synthesizer introduction before settling into a synth-pop arrangement, with Christian Purwien’s vocals staying restrained throughout. Heldautomat describe the track on Bandcamp as a song with “no metaphors, no way out, no redemption. Just the quiet realisation that things come to an end.” Purwien writes the lyrics and sings. Kowa plays the synthesizers. Olaf Wollschläger produced the single. Club mix and video for ‘Liebe ist endlich’ The digital release also includes a “Videomix” of the duo’s first single, “Am ersten Tag”, and a club mix of “Liebe ist endlich” produced by Purwien & Kowa, Purwien and Kowa’s other recording project. Liebe ist endlich by Heldautomat About Heldautomat Heldautomat is the Dortmund, Germany duo of Christian Purwien and Thomas Kowa, working with analogue synthesizers, piano and a drum machine alongside Purwien’s vocals. Purwien co-founded Second Decay in Witten in 1987 with Andreas Michael Sippel, after the pair had performed as Blue Velvet from 1985. Second Decay recorded entirely on analogue synthesizers and released albums including “Taste” (1994) and “The Hunt” (1998) before going quiet after 2002. Emmo.Biz Records has since reissued “The Hunt” on green double vinyl and “Taste” on a second double-LP edition. The duo played the 18th Elektrisch Festival on February 27, 2026, in a set drawn 70 percent from Second Decay material. Heldautomat released its debut single, “Am ersten Tag“, on May 15, 2026. “Anders Sein” followed on August 14, reworking a song Sippel and Purwien wrote for Second Decay’s “Taste” in 1994. “Liebe ist endlich” is the third single, and precedes the October 23 album “Zwischen den Lichtern”, produced throughout by Olaf Wollschläger and including a cover of Nine Inch Nails‘ “Hurt”. A vinyl edition of the album, limited to 100 hand-signed copies, is available alongside the digital release.

items.body: Marilyn Manson’s second studio album, “Antichrist Superstar,” turns 30 this year. The band released the record on 8 October 1996 through Nothing and Interscope Records. A rock opera and concept album, it followed 1994’s “Portrait of an American Family” and the 1995 EP “Smells Like Children,” and was recorded over roughly eight months at Nothing Studios in New Orleans. The album was produced by Marilyn Manson together with Trent Reznor, Dave Ogilvie and Sean Beavan, with Ogilvie departing partway through the sessions and Beavan brought in to finish the record with the band. Guitarist Daisy Berkowitz left the group during recording and was replaced by Zim Zum shortly after the album’s completion, with bassist Twiggy Ramirez performing the majority of the guitar parts. The 16-track CD, split into three sections titled “The Heirophant,” “Inauguration of the Worm” and “Disintegrator Rising,” runs “Irresponsible Hate Anthem,” “The Beautiful People,” “Dried Up, Tied and Dead to the World,” “Tourniquet,” “Little Horn,” “Cryptorchid,” “Deformography,” “Wormboy,” “Mister Superstar,” “Angel with the Scabbed Wings,” “Kinderfeld,” “Antichrist Superstar,” “1996,” “Minute of Decay,” “The Reflecting God” and “Man That You Fear,” followed by a hidden track, “Empty Sounds of Hate.” Album artwork was designed by P. R. Brown using photography by Dean Karr. “Antichrist Superstar” debuted at number three on the Billboard 200 and has sold close to two million copies in the United States. Lead single “The Beautiful People” preceded the album on 22 September 1996 and reached number 26 on Billboard’s Modern Rock Tracks chart and the top 20 of the UK Singles Chart, followed by second single “Tourniquet” on 8 September 1997, which peaked at number 28 in the UK. The album is the first installment of a trilogy the band completed with “Mechanical Animals” (1998) and “Holy Wood (In the Shadow of the Valley of Death)” (2000), and was supported by the year-long Dead to the World Tour. About Marilyn Manson Marilyn Manson formed in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, in 1989, when singer Brian Warner – who took the stage name Marilyn Manson – paired with guitarist Scott Putesky, known as Daisy Berkowitz. Performing initially as Marilyn Manson & the Spooky Kids, the group built a South Florida following through theatrical live shows, with a lineup that came to include bassist Brad Stewart (Gidget Gein), keyboardist Stephen Bier (Madonna Wayne Gacy) and drummer Fred Streithorst (Sara Lee Lucas). In 1993, Nine Inch Nails founder Trent Reznor signed the band as the first act on his Nothing Records label and produced their debut album, “Portrait of an American Family,” released on 19 July 1994. The “Smells Like Children” EP followed in 1995, featuring a cover of the Eurythmics’ “Sweet Dreams (Are Made of This)”; Jeordie White, performing as Twiggy Ramirez, had by then replaced Gein on bass. “Antichrist Superstar” followed on 8 October 1996, co-produced by Reznor, Marilyn Manson, Dave Ogilvie and Sean Beavan, and debuted at number three on the Billboard 200 behind lead single “The Beautiful People.” The album’s success coincided with the departure of founding guitarist Daisy Berkowitz and the arrival of Zim Zum, and the band supported the record with the Dead to the World Tour. The group’s next album, “Mechanical Animals,” arrived on 15 September 1998, followed by “Holy Wood (In the Shadow of the Valley of Death)” in 2000, closing out the self-described triptych that “Antichrist Superstar” opened. Thirty years after its release, the album remains the first chapter of that trilogy.

items.body: Front Line Assembly’s “Epitaph” turns 25 this year. Metropolis Records released the electro-industrial and EBM album on 8 October 2001, the eleventh full-length studio album by the Vancouver band led by Bill Leeb and Chris Peterson. The record marked Front Line Assembly‘s return to Metropolis Records after the band left the label in October 1999. “Epitaph” runs ten tracks and 54:57, recorded at Cryogenic Studio and produced by Leeb and Peterson. Greg Reely handled mixing and engineering, Brian Gardner mastered the album, and Dave McKean supplied the artwork and design. The tracklist runs “Haloed”, “Dead Planet”, “Backlash”, “Epitaph”, “Everything Must Perish”, “Conscience”, “Decoy”, “Insolence”, “Krank It Up” and “Existance”, the last of which folds in the hidden track “Submerged” after a minute of silence. Metropolis also issued a digipak edition limited to 25,000 copies carrying that bonus track. “Everything Must Perish”, released 11 September 2001, was the only single taken from the album. Bill Leeb told Side-Line at the time that “Epitaph” broke with the band’s earlier reliance on film dialogue samples: “This is the first time we quit using movie samples.” He added: “Sampling is an artform which was criticised in the beginning, but now it’s a respected artform with big money in it. It’s a big business where I don’t feel at ease any longer.” Artoffact Records re-released ‘Epitaph’ on limited edition vinyl in 2015. About Front Line Assembly Bill Leeb founded Front Line Assembly in Vancouver, British Columbia, in 1986 after leaving Skinny Puppy, where he had performed under the stage name Wilhelm Schroeder. Rhys Fulber worked with Leeb from the same period as an early, unofficial collaborator, and Michael Balch became an official member on keyboards and programming in 1988. The band’s debut album, “The Initial Command”, came out on the Belgian label KK at the end of 1987, followed by “State of Mind” on the German label Dossier in January 1988 and “Corrosion” the same year, licensed to Wax Trax! for North America. Balch left after the Gashed Senses & Crossfire tour in 1989 to join Ministry and Revolting Cocks, and Fulber stepped in as an official member. “Gashed Senses & Crossfire” (1989) gave the band its first chart entry, with “Digital Tension Dementia” reaching No. 45 on Billboard’s Hot Dance Club Songs. “Caustic Grip” followed in 1990, the album that began Front Line Assembly’s long-running partnership with mixer and engineer Greg Reely and introduced more guitar-driven material. Chris Peterson debuted as a live percussionist on the accompanying tour before later becoming a full-time member. “Tactical Neural Implant” (1992) brought a more melodic, sample-heavy direction, and “Millennium” (1994) became the band’s first industrial metal record, featuring session guitar from Devin Townsend, who also played on “Hard Wired” (1995). Fulber left in 1997 to concentrate on producing Fear Factory, and Peterson took over his role as the band moved toward the electronica and big-beat leanings of “[FLA]vour of the Weak” (1997) and “Implode” (1999). In October 1999 the band left Metropolis Records; “Epitaph”, produced by Leeb and Peterson and issued on 8 October 2001, marked its return to that label. Peterson departed after finishing work on the album, and Fulber rejoined in 2003 for “Civilization” (2004). Beyond the main discography, Leeb has led the side project Delerium since 1987, and members have worked on Noise Unit, Conjure One (Fulber), Cyberaktif (Leeb with Skinny Puppy’s cEvin Key and Dwayne Goettel) and other spin-offs. Front Line Assembly went on to release “Artificial Soldier” (2006), “Improvised Electronic Device” (2010), “Echogenetic” (2013), “Wake Up the Coma” (2019) and “Mechanical Soul” (2021), the last featuring guest appearances from Jean-Luc De Meyer of Front 242 and Dino Cazares of Fear Factory. The band caught up with Side-Line on the state of the group in 2024, with Leeb and Fulber both still in the current lineup. “Epitaph” remains the band’s eleventh studio album and, twenty-five years on, the record that reopened its relationship with Metropolis Records.

About Ms Xxan Ms Xxan writes, performs and produces spoken word and industrial noise music from Berkeley, California. She released the nine-track spoken word dark ambient album “Make Yourself the Lie” on September 8, 2026, as a free, name-your-price download via VūMantra Records, the Berlin label founded in 2019 by Vince Gagliardi, who also records as The Nent and LAGÁN. That album carried a content warning for explicit lyrics addressing depression, and the same material also circulates as a podcast on Apple Podcasts and Audiomack. Ms Xxan handles writing, performance, composition and production on her own across both releases. With “shaper of decrepitude.”, she returned to self-releasing directly on Bandcamp, pairing the title track with “ghosted.” as a quick follow-up to the VūMantra album.

items.body: This third album from the mysterious Swiss duo Blackbook was released just before the summer and brings us a total of 12 new tracks. I have always been somewhat intrigued by this act. While their music sounds superb, it is invariably driven by massive clichés and often seems almost literally ‘lifted’ from existing songs. With “Different”, they remain true to their 80s Electro-Wave/Pop influences, yet the tracks sound somewhat more personal this time around. It may be a cliché, but the way they develop their sound—consistently delivering strong choruses—is remarkable. Every single track sounds danceable and powerful, possessing the essential catchiness this genre demands. The songs also appear to have been deliberately kept short—not a single one reaches the four-minute mark. Blackbook remains a true mystery, yet one that consistently returns with great music—clichéd or not! (Rating:8½). Listen to “Nobody Loves You”: Nobody Loves You by Blackbook About Blackbook Blackbook is a Swiss duo who perform under masks and withhold their surnames, going only by their first names, Matthias and Albert. Both had previously played in other Swiss and German acts before forming Blackbook, citing 80s and 90s music as a shared influence. The duo discussed their approach and anonymity in a Side-Line interview in 2023. The project released a series of singles before compiling them into its official debut album, “Confessions Of The Innocent” (2023), followed by “Radio Strange” (2024) and, issued just before the summer of 2026, the duo’s third album “Different”, all released through darkTunes Music Group.

items.body: Simple Minds released their twelfth studio album, “Neon Lights”, on 8 October 2001 through Eagle Records. The Scottish post-punk and new wave band’s collection of cover versions turns 25 this year, arriving as the group’s first release after a period away from active recording. “Neon Lights” was conceived as a warm-up ahead of the following year’s “Cry” and gathers Simple Minds’ versions of songs by artists including Them, David Bowie, Pete Shelley, the Patti Smith Group, Kraftwerk, the Doors, Echo and the Bunnymen, Neil Young, Roxy Music and the Velvet Underground. Frontman Jim Kerr set out the thinking behind the project at the time of release: “Neon Lights is the first time Simple Minds have put together a collection of non-original material. We thought it was appropriate at a period of looking back that we go to the very foundations of Simple Minds, which of course is the music and the bands who influenced us.” The album followed a difficult stretch for the band. Their prior record, “Our Secrets Are the Same”, had been delivered to Chrysalis but was caught up in the label’s merger with EMI, remained unreleased, and was then leaked on the internet in 2000. Discouraged by the lost momentum, band members Eddie Duffy, Mark Taylor and Mark Kerr moved on to other projects, and Jim Kerr relocated to Sicily to work part-time as a hotelier. In 2001, Kerr and guitarist Charlie Burchill began working with multi-instrumentalist Gordon “Gordy” Goudie, a former member of the Primevals, on new material intended for “Cry”. Recorded in parallel with those sessions in Glasgow, Dublin and Taormina, Sicily, “Neon Lights” was completed and released first. Simple Minds’ ‘Neon Lights’ tracklist and credits The UK edition ran ten tracks: “Gloria” (Them), “The Man Who Sold the World” (David Bowie), “Homosapien” (Pete Shelley), “Dancing Barefoot” (Patti Smith Group), “Neon Lights” (Kraftwerk), “Hello, I Love You” (the Doors), “Bring on the Dancing Horses” (Echo and the Bunnymen), “The Needle and the Damage Done” (Neil Young), “For Your Pleasure” (Roxy Music) and “All Tomorrow’s Parties” (the Velvet Underground). A US release added two further covers, “Being Boiled” (the Human League) and “Love Will Tear Us Apart” (Joy Division). The album was produced by Jim Kerr and Charlie Burchill with Gordy Goudie, except for “Gloria”, which was produced by Phunk Investigation, Daniele Tignino and Emiliano Patrik Legato; Simon Heyworth handled mastering. Two singles followed the album: the “Dancing Barefoot” EP and a series of “Homosapien” remixes. The full album is available via Spotify. About Simple Minds Simple Minds trace back to Johnny and the Self-Abusers, a Glasgow punk band formed in early 1977 by Jim Kerr, Charlie Burchill, Tony Donald and Brian McGee. That group released a single, “Saints and Sinners”, on Chiswick Records in November 1977 and split the same day. The remaining members regrouped under the name Simple Minds, drawn from a lyric in David Bowie’s “The Jean Genie”, and played their first show on 17 January 1978 in Glasgow. Duncan Barnwell joined on second guitar that January, Mick MacNeil added keyboards in March, and Derek Forbes replaced Donald on bass in April; Barnwell left by November, leaving a settled quintet of Kerr, Burchill, MacNeil, Forbes and McGee. Manager Bruce Findlay signed the band to Zoom Records, licensed to Arista, for a 1979 debut, “Life in a Day”, which reached number 30 on the UK Albums Chart. Further albums followed in quick succession: “Real to Real Cacophony” (1979), “Empires and Dance” (1980) and the double release “Sons and Fascination” / “Sister Feelings Call” (1981). Brian McGee left after those sessions and was eventually replaced by Mel Gaynor, recruited by producer Peter Walsh in 1982 and later the band’s longest-standing drummer. Released from Arista in early 1981, Simple Minds signed to Virgin Records, and “New Gold Dream” (1982) gave the band its first Billboard 200 entry and a number 3 UK placing. “Sparkle in the Rain” (1984) debuted at number 1 in the UK and was later certified Platinum, and “Once Upon a Time” (1985) reached number 1 in the UK and the Netherlands and was certified triple Platinum in Britain, driven by the US number 1 single “Don’t You (Forget About Me)” from the film “The Breakfast Club”. Bassist Derek Forbes was dismissed in the mid-1980s and replaced by John Giblin, who debuted at Live Aid in 1985. “Street Fighting Years” (1989) topped the UK chart despite Gaynor and Giblin leaving mid-session, and keyboardist Mick MacNeil quit at the close of the subsequent tour. “Real Life” (1991) and “Good News from the Next World” (1995) followed as the band’s lineup narrowed to the core of Kerr and Burchill, with Forbes and Gaynor rejoining in 1996 and 1997 respectively. “Neapolis” (1998) was the band’s only album released through Chrysalis Records. By the time of “Neon Lights” (2001), the band had regrouped around Kerr, Burchill and new recruit Gordy Goudie, who remains in the lineup today. “Cry” followed in 2002, backed by the band’s first North American tour in seven years. Simple Minds went on to release “Black & White 050505” (2005), “Graffiti Soul” (2009), which gave the band its first UK top 10 album in 14 years, “Big Music” (2014), “Acoustic” (2016), “Walk Between Worlds” (2018) and “Direction of the Heart” (2022) through BMG. The band’s catalogue has topped 60 million albums sold worldwide, and its accolades include the 2016 Ivor Novello Award for Outstanding Song Collection and the 2014 Q Inspiration Award. The current lineup pairs founders Kerr and Burchill with Goudie, Sarah Brown, Ged Grimes, Cherisse Osei and Erik Ljunggren; in September 2026 the band announced a new studio album, “Sacrosanct”, due for release on 29 January 2027. Twenty-five years after “Neon Lights”, the covers album remains the clearest record of the influences, from Kraftwerk to Joy Division, that shaped the band’s own sound.

items.body: We all want something better, bright and shiny dust. Fake names to hide within, blind among the rust Northeastern Pennsylvania has always seemed peculiarly suited to its own species of Gothic, where abandoned coal mines, crumbling factories, old churches, and stubborn little towns exist in uneasy communion with the American Dream. There is something metaphysically peculiar about a landscape whose prosperity was excavated from beneath its own feet, leaving the earth hollow and its inhabitants contemplating what remains. Here, the Gothic requires neither medieval castles nor European aristocrats. It grows naturally from industrial decay, Catholic guilt, Appalachian folklore, and the peculiar American talent for building civilizations atop buried disasters. Under such circumstances, making strange, sinister music seems less like an artistic decision than a perfectly reasonable response to one’s surroundings. Which brings us to ZEU, pronounced “zoo,” the musical alter ego of Matthew Zedolik of Wilkes-Barre, who has apparently decided that the region’s accumulated ghosts could use a backing band. There are few things more dangerous to public decency than a man left alone in a recording studio with a guitar, a head full of questionable ideas, and absolutely nobody around to tell him when to stop. Sometimes the result is genius. Zedolik writes, plays, records, and produces everything himself, an arrangement capable of yielding either magnificent obsession or twelve tracks of a man arguing with his presets. Fortunately, he seems to have made peace with his machinery, although his relationship with the rest of civilization remains questionable. Zedolik describes his approach as “’80s-era Springsteen meets Billy Idol, Depeche Mode, and Sisters of Mercy.” Which sounds like a barroom dare issued after somebody fed the jukebox three dollars and locked all the exits. Imagine the Boss borrowing Andrew Eldritch’s wardrobe, Billy Idol stealing the getaway car, and Martin Gore sitting in the back seat contemplating several regrettable romantic decisions. On Blind Among The Rust and Beyond Life and Death, ZEU takes that peculiar family reunion somewhere considerably less respectable. The songs inhabit the cracked asphalt between Tom Waits and The Gun Club, with the skeletal guitar menace of Rowland S. Howard and the diseased theatrical instincts of Foetus lurking nearby. There is something wonderfully disreputable about the combination, a species of surf goth that sounds as though somebody dragged a rockabilly band through a cemetery and subsequently denied them access to decent amplifiers. Zedolik’s growling vocals come crawling out of the arrangements with the nicotine-stained authority of a man who has seen the bottom of several bottles and found the conversation there surprisingly agreeable. Echoing guitars suggest desert highways, abandoned dance halls, and the occasional questionable roadside establishment, while atmospheric synthesizers introduce an industrial chill. Beneath the Gothic furnishings sits a garage-rock impulse, loose enough to suggest spontaneous combustion and sufficiently disciplined to keep the songs from collapsing into glorious nonsense. His musical education explains some of this strange chemistry. Teenage metal bands supplied the muscle; The Ordinals taught him bass discipline; American Buffalo Ghost gave him considerable guitar mileage. Recording studies in New York subsequently sharpened his understanding of arrangement and spatial dynamics. The accumulated experience gives these recordings their peculiar sense of purpose, even when the music appears headed toward some spectacularly unpleasant destination. Listen below: Blind Among The Rust / Beyond Life and Death by Zeu Following July’s full-length Existor, these two singles, released through Everything Evaporated, suggest an artist increasingly comfortable inhabiting his own peculiar corner of Pennsylvania Gothic. Somewhere between the last call at a roadside tavern and the first light over a neglected graveyard, ZEU has found a promising place to conduct his business. The neighbours may have complaints. items.body: Silence has a talent for passing itself off as peace. Two people can share a room, exchange the necessary pleasantries, and conduct an entire argument without troubling the air between them. Inside, every withheld accusation is already gathering speed. Given enough time, even “How was your day?” can begin to sound like a contact sport. Milan quartet October take that condition onto the ice in their video for Universe. The fourth single from their debut album, Dancing Like an Idiot, out now through Waddafuzz! Records, follows the uncomfortable distance between what a relationship looks like from the outside and what its participants are putting themselves through within it. A frozen surface can conceal considerable commotion, and October have enlisted a hockey team to give those private collisions a public airing. The song itself has a supple, sophisticated swing. A rhythmic bassline brings the new wave funk of Roxy Music and Japan to mind, its firm articulation keeping the groove grounded as sustained guitar tones stretch above it. The snare lands at deliberate intervals, leaving generous space around each strike. There is a progressive streak in the arrangement, a willingness to let the instrumental passages stretch and change shape without losing the underlying rhythm. Gianluca Villa sings in a silky upper register reminiscent of Peter Gabriel, his measured delivery building to increasingly impassioned peaks on the line “A Message from the stars.” A gentle guitar jangle carries the song forward, lifting some of its emotional weight. A string interlude zigzags through the arrangement as the vocal rises into a high croon, and tension builds until the full force of the performance comes crashing back. Directed and edited by Fabrizio Grasso, with concept and production by Davide Debenedetti for Filmico, the video makes that division visible. October perform on the rink beneath bright backlights, framed against rows of empty seats, while members of Sgularat Hockey Club Milano skate around them in yellow and black. The musicians hold their positions as the players accelerate, compete, and cut across the space between them. Pads, helmets, and sticks give anger and frustration a physical vocabulary; the ice supplies the emotional temperature. There is something both funny and painfully apt about bringing protective equipment into a love song. Here, the action surrounding the band becomes the argument nobody is having aloud: misunderstandings, thwarted attempts at connection, and the helplessness of trying to reach someone who has become difficult to recognise. Grasso lets the rink carry the metaphor, its broad white expanse accommodating all that activity without offering much warmth. Watch the video for Universe below: October formed in Milan in 2024, bringing together musicians whose backgrounds include Grandi Animali Marini, Il Fieno, NOA, and Egokid, alongside collaborations with Veracrash and I Ministri. Villa handles guitar and vocals, joined by bassist Dario Giordano, drummer Paolo Soffientini, and synth player Davide “dEbE” Debenedetti. Their debut was recorded at Casamedusa with Francesco Campanozzi and Frigo Studio with Francesco Ferrari, then mixed and mastered by Paolo Mauri. Released on March 30, 2026, Dancing Like an Idiot is available digitally and on vinyl. Listen to Universe below and order the album here. items.body: There is a particular kind of youthful ambition that treats a synthesizer’s limitations as somebody else’s problem. If the arrangement feels crowded, another drum track might settle the argument; if the equipment begins to struggle, perhaps it needs to be programmed harder. Baltimore’s Pygmy Children remember their earliest recordings with the affectionate candor of two people who have since learned exactly what they were putting their machines through. More than thirty years later, those experiments are getting a fresh listen. Out now through Re:Mission Entertainment, Malignant: Redux revisits the electro-industrial duo’s 1994 debut album, Malignant, and the preceding 1993 EP, Facedown. Released October 2, the collection brings brothers Pete and Brian Roper back to the recordings that introduced them to the American industrial underground, with the digital edition collecting both releases in full. Originally recorded at Hit and Run Studios in Rockville, Maryland, with engineer Steve Carr, the material has received its first official remaster from Jeff Mortimer at JM Mastering. Brian Roper supplies the Redux artwork, completing a return to a period when the duo’s appetite for dense arrangements regularly outpaced the resources at their disposal. The brothers describe those sessions with refreshing frankness: “Admittedly, the record sounds pretty raw. We were novices trying to create something multi-layered and frenetic, working with what we had and probably not fully knowing what the hell we were doing, just going for it. Some of the synths were being pushed to the point of voice exhaustion, while multiple drum tracks pounded away simultaneously. Looking back, some editing was probably in order, but the intention was always there. We may not have hit the target exactly, but the aim was definitely there.” That willingness to admit the excess is part of the appeal. Their account describes two musicians learning through accumulation, pursuing an idea until the equipment itself began to object. The early titles suggest a similarly restless approach: Core moves between Resistance and Meltdown, while Facedown appears in Reflex, Manic, Bootstamp, and Dead versions across the digital collection. Even the track listing seems reluctant to leave an experiment alone. For Re:Mission founder Wes Turner, the release also carries a personal connection. Pygmy Children helped shape his taste in dark electronic music during the 1990s; three decades on, his label is releasing both their new work and these formative recordings. Turner now gets to put the records that helped educate him back into other listeners’ hands. Listen to Malignant : Redux below: Malignant : Redux by Pygmy Children Pygmy Children first surfaced with Facedown on Noname/Noslogan Productions, following it with Malignant before moving on to Deconstruct, released by Cleopatra in 1995, and Low Life Dream, issued through Sub/Mission Records and Out Of Line in 1998. After years away, the brothers returned in 2025 through Re:Mission with Coincidental Strategies, accompanied by singles including I Have No Name and Signal Unknown. Their recent single Proof in Lies, which we covered in August, leads their forthcoming fifth studio album, Into The Silence. With new material underway, Malignant : Redux offers a timely return to the duo’s beginnings. The brothers can now afford to smile at their early excesses, though the synthesizers they used back then may still be entitled to an apology. Malignant : Redux is available digitally and on CD via Re:Mission Entertainment. Order here or find additional listening options here. Digital edition: Both Malignant and Facedown in full, comprising 16 tracks. Limited digipak CD: An edition of 100 copies, containing Malignant plus Fear, the B-side from the Facedown EP, with the digital edition included. Three-CD autographed bundle: Malignant : Redux alongside autographed original pressings of Malignant and Facedown, plus the digital edition. Limited to 25 bundles, with US shipping only. items.body: 2026.10.08 東京交響楽団2027/28シーズンラインナップ発表記者会見が開催！ 2年目は「危険な年」？ 2026年10月7日、ミューザ川崎シンフォニーホールで行なわれた東京交響楽団の2027／28シーズンラインナップ発表記者会見に、音楽監督ロレンツォ・ヴィオッティが登壇した。 2026／27シーズンから音楽監督に就任し、その任期が2034年3月までの延長が発表されたばかりのヴィオッティ。「まだこの第1シーズンの最中にはありますが、もうすでに楽団員はもちろんのこと、スタッフ、そして合唱団、すべての方々を私は心から誇りに思っています」と切り出した。 その実感を強くしたのが、9月に演奏したフランツ・シュミット《七つの封印の書》だった。「本当に素晴らしい演奏をしてくれました。特に合唱団は、あたかも簡単な作品であるかのように演奏してくれました。でも、実際にはもっとも難しいと言っていい作品です」。 そんな現在地から、2027／28シーズンにさらに大きな挑戦となるのが演奏会形式で上演するワーグナーの《ローエングリン》だ。「ステージのないワーグナー作品というのは、一見難しいように思われますが、《ローエングリン》は、皆さんがちょっと目をつぶって、音楽に耳を傾けていただければ、その情景の動きをありありと思い浮かべることができるオペラの一つではないかと思っています」。 シュミット作品のみならず、ヴェルディやブラームスのレクイエムを経て挑むワーグナーは、「これまで積み重ねてきた経験がすべて大きく実って、それがつながっていく作品」だと語った。 ロレンツォ・ヴィオッティ 1990年スイス・ローザンヌ出身。カダケス国際指揮者コンクール、ライプツィヒMDR指揮者コンクールなどで優勝し、2015年ザルツブルク音楽祭にてネスレ・ヤング・コンダクター賞を受賞。グルベンキアン管弦楽団首席指揮者（2018～2021）、ネーデルラント・フィルハーモニー管弦楽団およびオランダ国立歌劇場首席指揮者（2021～2025）を歴任。これまでにウィーン・フィル、ベルリン・フィル、ロイヤル・コンセルトヘボウ管、ライプツィヒ・ゲヴァントハウス管、ベルリン・シュターツカペレ、ミュンヘン・フィル、ロサンゼルス・フィル、クリーヴランド管などを指揮。オペラにおいてもウィーン国立歌劇場、パリ・オペラ座、ミラノ・スカラ座などに客演し、高い評価を得ている。 2014年、東京交響楽団との共演で日本デビュー。初共演から10年を迎えた2024年８月、東京交響楽団次期音楽監督に任命され、2026/27シーズンより第4代音楽監督に就任。2028年8月からはチューリッヒ歌劇場音楽総監督に就任する。 ©︎N.Ikegami また、音楽監督2年目にあたる来シーズンについては、「2年目こそ、ある意味での脆さが出やすい、危険性をはらんだ年になります。しかし、少しずつ相手のことがわかり始めると、当然ながら“小さなぶつかり”も出てくる。実はこれはこれで大切なことだと私は思っています」と述べた。 「私の任期も3年から8年へと延びました。長くいると、もっともっと音楽を掘り下げ、より高い質と、より多く、広く、深くということが可能になってくると思っています。これからの8年をかけて、できることすべてをする気持ちでいます。より強く、よりよい関係を築いていきたい」と力を込めた。 マーラー、ストラヴィンスキー、シューマンともっと音楽を深く掘る その関係を築いていくために、具体的にはどのようなプログラムが組まれるのか。ヴィオッティが会見で特に注目したのは、マーラー、ストラヴィンスキー、そしてシューマンだった。 今シーズンにすでに演奏したマーラーの交響曲第1番は、「新しい世界の幕開けを思わせる」作品。「本当にその、非常に音楽に対する献身と想像力、そして思い切り、すべてが求められる作品です」。そして来シーズンには交響曲第7番をとりあげる。マーラーが作曲において「和声や作曲技法において挑戦した作品と言える。技術的にも決して簡単ではない」と、オーケストラにとっても大きな挑戦になることを明かした。 そしてストラヴィンスキーについては「私の心にもっとも近い作曲家の一人で、その音色の探求を、東京交響楽団とともにできることを楽しみにしております」と期待を込めた。 最後に、シーズン終盤に置かれるのがシューマンだ。「数週間前に『今、もっとも心にある作曲家は？』と質問されて、シューマンと答えました」。ヴィオッティにとってシューマンは、重くなりすぎてもいけない。一方で、古典的に軽くなりすぎてもいけないそう。「このバランスをオーケストラとともに模索していくことが一つの課題になると思っています」。 来シーズンのイメージカラーと同じバーガンディ色のセーターをお召しのヴィオッティ監督 ヴァイオリニストの佐藤俊介がクリエイティブ・パートナーに 2027年4月から3年間、ヴァイオリニストの佐藤俊介が東京交響楽団クリエイティブ・パートナーに就任することも発表されている。ヴィオッティはまだ直接会ったことはないが、オランダのオーケストラで楽団員から話を聞き、SpotifyやYouTubeなどで彼の演奏を聴いているという。 「非常に好印象を抱いています。オーケストラとしても、室内楽的に、お互いに親密によく聴き合う姿勢は、とても大事なんです。そのような意味でも彼を迎えるのは大きな意味を持つと思っています」 廣岡楽団長からは、佐藤との活動を通して、指揮者を置かずに一緒に演奏するような取り組みや、バロック音楽のアプローチ、さらにはこれまでオーケストラが取り組んでこなかったジャンルとのコラボレーションへの期待も語られた。 items.body: “Rub’a’Dub Love” is 8-bit digital reggae in the style of the 1980s, and it originally appeared on the album Where My Style Comes From, released in June. On 2 October it came back in two remixes on UK-based digital dub and reggae label Superchip: raggamuffin boom-bap from Hopebullet, a DJ and sound engineer from Osaka who also goes by Ranking Jin, and a second version by RJD. Behind it are deejay Daddy Cookiz and producer Simma, with singer Ponchita Peligros as guest. Simma is Nathan Simm from Hull, England, a producer and DJ who started out in Ableton during the 2020 lockdown, runs Superchip and also records as Polyecho and Square Nath. His 2024 debut, Simma Enters The Game, mixed digital reggae, dubbed-out hip-hop and 8-bit chiptune and drew on the German label Jahtari and the Scottish sound system Mungo’s Hi Fi. Daddy Cookiz has deejayed since 2005 and grew up on Jamaican sound system culture, and he takes his cues from Super Cat, Yellowman and Shabba Ranks. On the album he deejays in that rub-a-dub tradition over Simma’s digital sound, and Simma now takes that sound to Japan, where he performs with Hopebullet in Kyoto on 10 October, Tokyo on 19 October and Yokohama on 21 October, in a showcase for Superchip. items.body: 『声なき声のドローイング:スキャン画像』2026［© Shu Yonezawa, Courtesy of SNOW Contemporary］ 会期：2026/07/17～2026/09/05 会場：SNOW Contemporary［東京都］ 公式サイト：http://snowcontemporary.com/exhibition/202607.html （前編から） ステートメントには続けて「彩度は低く細かな色相の差異で描いたのはキャラクターと捉えるには薄く複雑な声未満の存在であ」ったと書かれている。米澤は以前から、キャラクターの「声」に関心を寄せてきた。実際、キャラクターのアイデンティティを規定するうえで声はイメージと同等以上に重要な役割を果たしているだろう。しかし米澤が声に見出しているのは、もっと広い可能性であるようにも思われる──アニマとキャラクターのあいだを自由に往還する現象としての可能性を。 そもそも“anima”が「魂」と同時に「息」や「風」を意味する語であったことを思い出そう。 神が息を吹き込むこと （ インスピレーション ） によって事物はアニメートされる。世界を巡る空気の流れが振動としてあらわれたものが声だと考えるなら、それはまさにアニマをもっとも色濃く反映した現象だと言えるだろう。無論、この魂-呼吸-声といった直線的な繋がりは、あくまでも西欧的な生命観にもとづくものであることに注意しなければならない。例えばアーティストの布施琳太郎は、米澤が描く「オバケ」状のキャラクターにおいてしばしば口が身体（構造）から遊離していることを指摘し、ここにアニマと声のより自由な関係の可能性を見ている★3。すなわち、ヤツメウナギなどに代表される無顎類が摂食のための口と呼吸のための鰓を完全に独立して発達させたように、米澤のキャラクター表現は、私たちが生物学的な人体構造によって規定されているがゆえに硬直してしまったアニマとの関係性を、いまひとたびときほぐすことを試みているのではないか、と★4。 自由に泳ぎ回る口があらゆる場所で開き、声を発する。もはやこのとき、「口」を画面内に描かれた身体パーツのみに限定する理由はない。むしろ米澤作品はつねに「口」そのものとともに存在してきたとも言えるだろう——フレームという口として。キャンバス、トレーシングペーパー、ビニール、モニタ、スクリーン——手法や素材の別によらず、米澤の作品は基本的に矩形の画面を前提としているように見える。特に本展では、これまでビニール自体をピンで固定する形式を主としてきた「アニマの通り跡」シリーズがアルミフレームに張られ、壁や空中に吊られている。また、映像を主とするインスタレーション的な作品《別の海としての身体》では、小型のモニタが半透明のアクリルケースによってさらにフレーミングされ、スピーカー——もっとも象徴的な機械の口——だけが隣接する壁面にさまよい出ている。とはいえ、アニメーション表現を背景に持つ米澤が矩形のフレームを意識するのは当然のことであり、そうした強固な枠があればこそ、不定形に蠢くアニマたちの流出もまた強調されるのだ、と言うことはできるだろう。ではその上で、あらゆる場所に開かれるフレームを「口」とみなすことはどんな意味を持つのか。 ［撮影：木奥惠三］ そもそも人間の発生に限ってみても、口とは「顔に開いた穴」などではない。妊娠初期にあたる8週から12週ごろ、胎児の顔部では、周囲から伸び上がってきた突起が中央で癒合することによって口唇や口蓋がつくられ、口の輪郭が完成する。口とはほんらい、開くものではなく、意図的に閉じ損なったものなのだ。最初はすべてが穴であり、その穴が埋められていく過程で残された残余としてのみ、口は定義しうる。ここで、白川静が「口」という漢字の成り立ちについて唱えた次のような説が思い出される。いわく、口は人間の開いた口唇ではなく、祝詞をおさめる器（サイ）のかたちに由来するのだと。学問的な信憑性に疑問はあるものの、解釈としては興味深い。すなわち、口を漢字練習帳のマス目のような「文字の到来を待つ空白」そのものの象形として捉えるなら、それは「いまだ閉じられていないこと」それ自体を意味する。そしてその「閉じられていない」という事実こそが、声を召喚する。口が声を発するのではない。むしろあらかじめ世界に満ちているそれが、たまたま口が見出されたときに受信され、声としてあらわれるのだ。この意味において、世界のあちこちに口を見出すことはそのまま声を見出すことであり、米澤が言うところの「アニメーション」概念のもっとも素朴なかたちであるように思える★5。 最後に、広義の「口」の観点から、米澤の代表的なモチーフである目についても考えておこう。目の本質を眼球ではなく、それが収まる眼窩やまぶたといった立体的なフレームに置いてみると、そこにはひとつの水槽のようなものが浮かび上がってくる。眼球というアニマが泳ぐ、涙で満たされた水槽が。口が開閉するように、目はまばたきを行なう。まばたきは視界を寸断して不完全な視覚をつくり出すが、同時に眼球を涙液でコーティングし、目を開き続けることで生じる像のブレを修正してもいる。つまり、視覚をいくつものフレームに分割する行為によってこそ、眼球はかろうじて息をしている。まばたきとは、目に許されたただひとつの呼吸であり、同時にこの器官が「閉じ損ねている」ことの証でもある。では果たして、完全な視界＝ずっと目を開き続ける視界などというものはありえるのだろうか。もしありえるのならばそのとき、一体なにが見えるのだろうか。 ［撮影：木奥惠三］ ここまでの議論をふまえると、本展は展示室に開いた口から流れ込んだアニマたちが、室内のあちらこちらに思い思いの像をあらわしていくひとつの現象として捉えられる——その構造はさながら、写真機の原型としての「 暗い部屋 （ カメラ・オブスキュラ ） 」を思わせる。しかし冒頭で述べたとおり、本展はむしろ光で満たされた「明るい部屋」としてあらわれている。ただしそれは、事物の輪郭を切り分ける乾いた光ではなく、目を凝らすほどにそのイメージを滲ませる湿った光、水底で感じる明るさに近い。波間でゆらぎ、水を透過して散乱した光が絶えず私たちの目を幻惑する。言葉遊びを許すなら「 水妖の部屋 （ カメラ・オブ・スキュラ ） 」とでも言えようか。水妖&efDotアニマは気ままに水と光の中に溶けてまわり、そのゆらめきのあいだに身を翻す。あちこちで口が開いては何ごとかをつぶやき、また消え去っていく。私の口もそれにつられて開くのだが、ごぼごぼと水音を立てるばかりで上手く喋れない。いや、そこでは私の口を借りて水妖たちの声があらわれているのだ。私がまだその声を捉えることができないというだけで。ぱくぱくと単調に開閉を繰り返すだけの口の動きは、再生か逆再生かを区別できない。それゆえに、時間は渦を巻いてほどけていく。水に包まれた私の目はまばたきを忘れ、ただ見開かれている。 ★3──布施琳太郎「無顎類のアニマ：キャラクターアートの終焉の後で」（米澤柊『泳ぐ目たちのアーカイヴ』所収、2026） ★4──私たち人間を思わせる身体パーツや骨格構造をところどころに有しつつも、中心性は不確かで、不定形に広がっている──こうした米澤作品におけるキャラクターの比喩として、私がまっさきに思いついたのはホヤであった。ホヤは尾索動物に属し、私たち脊椎動物と比較的近縁の生物である。オタマジャクシ型の幼生時は脳や脊索を備え、遊泳しながら住処を探す。この時点では摂食を行なわないため口はなく（眼点や嗅覚細胞の原型は存在するものの）器官としての目や鼻もない。そして無事、岩などを見つけるとそこに固着し、よく知られたホヤの形になる。脳や脊索、眼点を失う代わりに大きな口が開き、水を漉し取って栄養を摂取するだけの存在となる。いわばホヤは、脊椎動物的な身体構造を幼生から成体までのタイムスケールのなかに散在させている生物として捉えられる。言い換えれば、ホヤを時間的に再構成したものとして人間を考えることもできるだろう。 ★5──ここまで見てきた要素をまとめると、米澤の作品は、暗黙化した身体感覚／構造を再構成することを通じて、私たちが不可知化してしまったアニマを汲み上げようとしているのだといえる。そこには目（視覚）や声（聴覚）に加え、手指のモチーフを通じた触覚的なイメージや、米澤が「イメージの骨／アニメーションの骨」といった言い回しで示唆する、抽象的な身体感覚なども含まれている。しかし、嗅覚的な要素に限ってはあまり読み取れない。そもそも、米澤の描くキャラクター表象において鼻の存在感はきわめて希薄だ。横顔においてわずかに隆起らしきものが確認できるが、正面顔では鼻、とりわけ鼻孔はほぼ捨象されている。鼻は脊椎動物に特有の器官であり、もともと大脳は嗅覚情報処理のために大きく発達したのだとも言われている。 鑑賞日：2026/07/25（土）

items.body: 『声なき声のドローイング:スキャン画像』2026［© Shu Yonezawa, Courtesy of SNOW Contemporary］ 会期：2026/07/17～2026/09/05 会場：SNOW Contemporary［東京都］ 公式サイト：http://snowcontemporary.com/exhibition/202607.html 「声なき声のキャラクター」は米澤柊による個展である。展示作品はすべて2026年の新作で、なかでも米澤がここ一年ほど取り組んでいるという油絵作品が全体の七割近くを占めている。画面はどれも彩度の低い色が細かく重ねられることで構成されており、その茫洋とした色彩の渦を眺めるうちに、人間めいた輪郭や骨格、目、手の残像といったものたちの印象がかろうじて浮かび上がってくる。これは直感的には、白飛びした視界を思わせた。眠りから醒めたときに誰しもが味わうように、暗がりから急に光に満ちた空間へと晒された視界は明順応が間に合わず白く飽和する。そしてそこから徐々に、事物の輪郭や色彩を取り戻していく。しかし本展において、その視界が完全に明瞭になることはない。作品のあいだを行き交うにしたがい、眼球を包む涙液そのものが白濁していくかのごとく、乳白色の闇がゆるやかに立ち込める。六本木の雑居ビルの薄暗がりを切り開いてあらわれる端正なホワイトキューブともあいまって、本展はどこまでも明るく、しかし──それゆえに──知覚の不完全性を露わにしている。では、そんな淡い光の中に漂っているものたちとは一体なんなのだろうか。 ［撮影：木奥惠三］ 繰り返し述べられてきた内容のため簡潔に触れるにとどめるが、多くの手法やメディウムを横断した米澤の制作には「アニマ（魂・生命性）」への関心が通底しており、とりわけ特徴的なのが「オバケ」への着目である。「オバケ」とはアニメーション制作において、あるフレームとフレームのあいだの動きを補完し、物体の動きをより活き活きとみせるためにあえて（静止画としては）崩れた描写を行なう技術を指す。実際、現時点における米澤作品のもっとも一般的なイメージとは、身体がほどけて散らばりつつあるかのような「オバケ」としてのキャラクターたちの図像だろう。 画面内の事物を 息づかせ （ アニメートす ） るための技術が「オバケ」と呼ばれる逆説──いや、考えてみれば逆説ではないのだ。さまざまなアニメ作品において、「オバケ」のコマを単体で切り取ったスクリーンショットは作画崩壊の事例としてネットミーム化してきた。これはアニメーションの中割り技術への無知から生じた誤認にすぎないわけだが、ではなぜ人々が「オバケ」に対してそれほど強烈な印象を共有しえたのかといえば、なめらかなアニメーションのなかに「見てはいけないものを見てしまった」と感じたからにほかならないだろう。すなわち、「オバケ」とはアニメーションの物語時間を補填するために見逃され続けることを運命付けられた存在であり、それゆえ、ひとたび意識に上ったその姿は本物の怪異さながらに「ぞっとする」ものとなるのだ。 画面内におけるキャラクターの自律性が担保されるためには、無数の崩れかけた非-自律的な なにものか ・・・・・ が不可欠であるというジレンマ。米澤はこの主従──アニメーションを規定する所与の時間と、それを埋め合わせる「オバケ」という関係性──を撹乱する。ほんらい見てはいけないものである「オバケ」を一枚の図像──しかもモニタやキャンバスといったいかにも「見るべき」質感を帯びたもの──として固定したうえで、その身体の崩壊を過剰に押し進めていく。そのとき、アニメーションのなめらかさを整えるパテのごとき不定形な「オバケ」はフレームの隙間から這い出して、別の時間的秩序を育み始める──フレームレートに従って生起する単線的な物語とは異なる時間を。そこでは過去や未来は等しくまなざされ、因果もまた意味を失う。米澤はそうして、フレームとフレームのあいだの飛躍を補完するためにのみ生を許された存在に、 別種の生の可能性 （ アニマ ） を見ようとするわけだ。 このようにアニメーションをひとつの基点とする米澤の作品群は、その手法にかかわらず複雑な層性を帯びてきた。例えば米澤の代表的なシリーズである「オバケのスクリーンショット」では、現実の風景写真のなかに「オバケ」としてのキャラクターたちが描き込まれている。レイヤーの集合としてのデジタルペイントが現実の風景に重ね合わされ、しかもそれは連続する無数のフレームの一瞬を捉えた「スクリーンショット」として位置付けられる。こうした時間的・空間的な複層性のなかをたゆたう米澤の作品は、必然的に「いま・ここ」からの遊離を予感させる。イメージは確かに目の前に存在するはずなのに、どこかヴェールに包まれているような捉えどころのなさがついてまわる。それは失われたものへの憧憬なのか、来たるべきものの予兆なのか──無論、どちらでもありうる。先に述べたとおり、米澤が紡ごうとする非線形の時間的秩序のなかにおいて、過去・現在・未来は等価に立ち並んでいるのだから★1。アニマはつねに、現前と予感のあいだで見え隠れする。 この観点において、描画面をレイヤー状に切り分けるためのアナログな技術として油絵を位置付けることも可能だろう。しかし当然ながら、油絵においては絵具の乾燥状態が層を決定する。乾ききる前に次のストロークを置けば下の層は物理的に巻き込まれ、層と層の境界——それは時間的秩序そのものと言ってもいい——が相互に浸潤可能となる（もちろん、実際に米澤がそのような描法を用いたかどうかは問題ではない）。ここで層を決定しているのは描き手の意志ではなく、絵具の乾燥速度、すなわちメディウムに固有の時間である。フレームとフレームを繋ぐフラットな時間のあいだから、「オバケ」が棲まう異なる時間が這い出していったように、ここでは層と層のあいだにメディウム由来の液体的な時間感覚が流れ込んでいる★2。 ［撮影：斉藤桃加］ 本展のステートメント冒頭には「かたちを選んで描こうとするほど選ばなかったものを切りすててしまうようで息苦しく、絵は段々と白くなっていった」とある。幾重にもゆらぎながら仄かに浮かび上がる油彩のイメージは、さまざまな連想を喚起する。例えば長時間露光による写真。そこでは被写体が動くことによって輪郭がブレ、イメージは次第に発散へと向かっていく。あるいは拡散モデルにおける画像生成（を開始まもなく停止させたようす）。ここでは反対に、ブレの極点とでもいうべきノイズのなかに任意の輪郭が幻視され、イメージが浮かび上がってくる。輪郭が浮かび上がる前のさざめきと、輪郭が溶け去っていった後の残響。米澤の画面が置かれているのは、まさにその異なる二つのベクトルが調停され、判定が無化される地点／時点である。 米澤は「世界が意味になる前の複雑さについて考えたい」という。しかしここまで見てきたように「ほんらいの複雑な世界が、人間の手による記号的分節によって単純化されてしまう」という単線的な因果とは別の場所に向けてこそ、米澤の作品はひらかれているように思える。そういえば、私が米澤の油絵の画面からはじめに想起したもの。それは写真でもAIでもなく、ほとんど面影だけになってしまった記憶のことであった。限界まで薄れ抽象化された記憶は、それがどこに属するのかをもはや判別できず、ゆえに時間のあいだを自由に飛び回り、私たちの認識に影響を及ぼして回る。はじめて見たはずのものをなぜか懐かしく思うこと。反対に、何度も見たはずのものをなぜだか瑞々しく感じること。そうした認識の脱臼ともいうべき瞬間を真に受けて生き続けることが、可能であるように思えるのだ。米澤の作品世界においてならば。 ★1──個人的にここで想起するのは小林泰三「酔歩する男」である。作中では、一風変わったタイムトラベルの方法が描かれる。登場人物は「時間とは本来非連続なものであり、そこに連続性を見出しているのは私たちの脳である」との仮説を示し、実際に脳内の時間感覚を司る部位を破壊することで、さまざまな時間点をランダムに飛び回る存在となる。それは過去と未来が等しく可能性のなかに溶け込んだ非線形の人生であり、そこには始まりも終わりもありえない。 ★2──ここで思い出すのは、ジェフ・ウォールによるエッセイ「Photography and Liquid Intelligence」（1989）である。ウォールは、写真を織りなす光学と液体の緊張関係に焦点を当てた。つまりカメラという緻密な機械が生産する写真は、最終的に現像という液体の不確定性に晒されることで顕現するのであり、ウォールはここに乾いた近代的知性のオルタナティブとしての湿った知性、液体的知性を見るのである。エッセイはこの液体的知性をソラリスの海に喩えることで結ばれる。観測者の記憶からイメージを汲み出し反射させるその海には、結ばれる前のあらゆるイメージの素がたゆたいながら、こちらを見返しているわけだ。写真とは、現像液に潜む無数のイメージのひとつをたまさか拾い上げたものにすぎず、もう一度現像し直せばそこにはまったく違ったイメージが掬い取られるのかもしれない。フィルムを現像液に浸し続ければ、その還元力はやがて感光していない臭化銀にまで至り、あらゆるイメージを黒く塗りつぶしていく。それは白く飽和した油彩のイメージと対になるものだろう。 （後編へ） 鑑賞日：2026/07/25（土）
